text:
"Der Gott Aion," in Religwnsgeschichtliche Studien 192-230; Fauth, KP I ( 1979): 185-88;
A. 1. Baumgarten, The Phoenician History of Philo of Bybws, EPRO 89 (Leiden: Brill, 1981):
146-48; Marcel Le Glay, ''Aion," Lexicon Iconographicum Mythologiae Classicac vol. I/2
(Zurich and Munich: Artemis, 1981) 405.
AKRAMMACHAMAREI: This magical name, with variant spellings, occurs frequently in beneficent magical incantations in company with ABLANATHANALBA and SESENGENBARPHARANGES. For a possible explanation of the name from Hebrew, see G. Scholcm, Jewish
Gnosticism, Merkabah M_ysticism, and Talmudic Tradition (New York: The Jewish Theological
Seminary of America, 2 1965) 94-100.
Aktiophi( s): Hopfuer has suggested that this name is an epithet of Selene, goddess of the
moon, a name which occurs elsewhere in PGM (sec IV. 24 73, 2484, 2601, 2664, 2 749,
2913; VII. 317, 984; XVI. 23).
Ammon/Parammon: Hermes Parammon was honored as an Olympian god alongside Zeus
Ammon and Hera Ammonia. The epithet Parammon probably means "he next to Ammon."
Amon (Amoun): The Egyptian god Amon. See Bonnet, RARG 31-37, s.v. "Amun";
E. Otto, "Amun," Ldii I (1975): 237-48.
Anoch (Anog, anok): These letters, occurring often at the beginning of an invocation, correspond to the Egyptian ink (Coptic anok), "I am." Sec S. Sauneron, "Le Mondc du Magieien Egyptien," Le Montie du Sorcier (Paris 1966) 36-39.
Anouth: Name of Osiris (see Vil. 238,243,247; VIII. 83, 98-99, 102).
Anubis: Anubis is the jackal god of mummification, the son of Osiris and Nephthys. On
Anubis as key holder and guard ( PGM IV. 1465 ), see S. Morenz, "Anubis mit dcm Schlussel,"
Religion und Geschichte des al.ten Agypten (Kain: Bohlau, 1975) 510-20; J.-C. Grenier,
Anubis alexandrin aromain, EPRO 57 (Leiden: Brill, 1977); Jean Ledant, "Anubis," Lexiam
Iconographicum Mythologiac Classicae, vol. 1/2 (Zurich and Munich: Artemis, 1981) 862-73
and plates.
Aphrodite Ourania: "Heavenly Aphrodite," whose city is Aphroditopolis (Dendcra), refers
to Hathor; see Bleeker, Hathor and Thoth 46; Bonnet, RARG 277-82, s.v. "Hathor."
Apollonius ofTyana: This famous first-century philosopher/magician is the subject of an
extant biography by Philostratus. The attribution of a spell to him at PGM Xla. 1 is unique
in ancient magical literature. For a survey of the problems and bibliography, consult E. L.
Bowie, "Apollonius ofTyana: Tradition and Reality," ANRW II. 16. 2 (1978) 1652-99,
esp. 1686.
Apophis (Aphyphis): The "unseen serpent" (sec PGM IV. 190-91; cf. PGMIIl. 87) is Apophis, who is slain daily by Seth/Typhon in the barge of Ra. See E. Hornung and A.
Badawy, "Apophis, "Ldii l (1975): 350-52; Bonnet, RARG 51-53, s.v. "Apophis."
Archenthechtha (Harchentechtha): This is the Egyptian god Har-Khenty-Kher; cf. PGM
III. 170. Sec Bonnet, R.ARG 131-33, s.v. "Chentechtai"; U. R6sslcr-K6hler, "HorusChenteehtai," Ldii 3 (1980) :27-33. [R.K.R.]
Arsenophre: The Egyptian god Arsenouphis (note also PGM II. 117; IV. 1629; XII. 183;
XIXa. 7). Sec Bonnet, R.ARG 54-55, s.v. "Arsnuphis"; E. Winter, "Arsenuphis," LdA I
(1975) :424-25. [R.K.R.]
Arsentechtha (Harsentechtha): Perhaps the Egyptian name can be read Harscnncchtha,
"Horus, child of the strong one." [J.B.]
Arsentephtha: The name is probably Egyptian, "Horus, child of Ptah." [J.B.]
Artemis: In the PGM the goddess Artemis is identical with Selene, Hekate, and Persephone
(see also IV. 2523, 2720-21, 2816ff.; l.XXVIIl. 11-12, wirh a drawing of Artemis Multimammaea). The invocations to Artemis, however, do contain archaic elements of her original cult. Sec T. Hopfuer, "Hckate-Sclenc-Artemis und Verwandte in den griechischcn
Zaubcrpapyri und auf den Fluchtafdn," Pisciculi, Festschrift F. J Diilger (Miinster: Aschendorff, 1939) 125-45.
Assistant Daimon (paredros): Hellenistic magic knows of a special type of daimon called
pared1·os ("assistant" or "attendant spirit''). The name refers to a deity who has been summoned as a servant to carry out any number of specified magical tasks. Cf. also PGM IV

1348, 1841, 1851 (with parastates), 2083, 2109, 2145 (note); VII. 884; XII. 141f. and
surrounding contexts. See M. Eliade, Shamanism: Archaic Techniques ofEcstas_v, Bollingen Series 76 (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1964) 88-95; Hopfoer, OZ I, secs. lff;
C. Colpe, "Geister (Dii,monen)," RAC 10 ( 1974): 62lff.; C. Zintzen, "Paredros (paredms),"
KP 4 (1972): 510-11.
Astrapsouchos: According to Diogenes Laertius, Prooem. 2, Astrampsychos was the name
of one or several magicians·; sec E. Riess, "Astrampsychos," PRE 2 (1896): 179-80.
athor: Sec Hathor.
BAINCH666CH: This formula, which invokes the god whose name corresponds to "spirit
(soul) of darkness" (b3 n kky), occurs regularly in magical papyri and on curse tablets.
[R.K.R.] See Bonner, SMA. 26, 146; Bousset, Religinnsgeschichtliche Studien 224 and n. 23.
Balsames: This angelic name served originally as the name of a Phoenician sun god, but in
PGM IV. 1019 the god plays the role of a light divinity from heaven. Cf. XIl. 494. See A. 1.
Baumgarten, The Phoenician History of Philo ofByblos, EPRO 89 (Leiden: Brill, 1981) 14951, 185-86.
Basym: This magical name may have originally come from the Aramaic \vords meaning, "In
the name of. ..." For the magician, however, the word serves as a magical name. See
G. Alon,Jews,Judaism, and the Classical World (Jerusalem: Magnes Press, 1977) 235-51.
Baubo: Baubo may have originally come as an independent deity from Asia Minor, where
Hekatc also came from; she then entered into the circle of Demeter and the mysteries of
Eleusis. See W. Fauth, KP I, s.v. "Baubo."
Bear constellation: The identification of the constellation of the Bear with Artemis occurs
at PGM VII. 687. The Great Bear was believed to be Callisto, Artemis' fellow huntress,
who was transformed into a constellation. Callisto was a manifestation of Artemis herself,
who played an important role as a she-bear, especially at Brauronia. See also PGM IV. 1302;
VII. 862; XII. I 90; XIIb. 26; LXXIl. See W. Sale, "The Temple Legends of the Arkteia,"
RhM 118 (1975) :265-84; L. Kahl, "!.'Artemis de Brauron. Rites et mystcres," Antike
Kunst (1977): 86-98: W. Fauth, "Arktos in den griechischen Zauberpapyri, ZPE 57
(1984): 93-99.
Bes (Besa, Besas): Ancient Egyptian religion knew of an entire class of so-called Besdemons (in Greek, Bcsas), distinguished by their dwarf-sized ugliness, who served as protectors of sleep and childbirth. In Hellenistic Egypt, Bes became a pantheistic deity, and in this
form he appears in PGM VIL 222-49 and Vlll. 64-110 (sec also LXXXVIII: his plant, IV.
807). His role as an oracle giver was popular at Abydos (Ammianus Marcellinus 19. 12). In
PCM the god was idCntified also with the Headless One (sec n. on PCM II. 11 ). On Bes, sec
Bonnet, KARG 101-9; H. Altenmullcr, LdA I (1975): 720-24, with bibliography.
Biaiothanatos Daimon: The biaiothanatoi, those who died violent deaths, were unable to
enter the unden.vorld because their time on earth had not been completed. After death, they
lingered as evil spirits and were subject to magical compulsion. See J. H. Waszink, "Biothanati," RAC 2 (1954): 391-92.
Breathing stone; The magnet. Magnetism fascinated ancient philosophers and scientists,
who explained the phenomenon in a variety of ways. Already Thales explained it in magical
terms when he stated that '"life" (psyche) is in a magnet. Magnetic stones, not surprisingly,
played a great role in the magic of aU periods. See A. Barb, "La.pis Adamas," Hommages a
Marcel Renard, I (Bruxelles: Latomus, 1969) 67/f.
Bruno: For this epithet of Artemis of Pherai in Thessaly, see PGM IV. 2270, 2291, 2611,
2964; VII. 692; LXX. 20, where the epithet is attributed to Hekate, Selene, Persephone.
Etymologically, she is the "snorting'' and "angry'' and therefore "terrible" goddess of the
netherworld; cf. the command in PCM IV. 2247; Lucian, Necyom. 20. See 0. Kern, "Brimo,"
PRE 3 (1887): 853-54.
Chnouph (Chnoubis): The lion-headed serpent was popular in magic and is often found
pictured on amulets. The daimon is a syncretistic combination of the Egyptian creator god
Chnoum, the serpent Kneph, and the star Knm. In the PCM the name occurs mostly in voces
magicae, especially in the Harpon-Knouphi formula (see, e.g., PGM Ill. 435-36, 560-63;

RMG 135-40, s.v. "Chnum"; E. Orto, "Chnum," LdA 1 (1975) :950-54; Colpe, RAC 9
(1974): 619.
Daimon, pl. daimons: In the PGM, as often in Greek literature, this term is used of deities
and lesser spirits whose influential control is sought. In the New Testament, the word is used
of an evil spirit, "demon," a sense not generally used in the PGM.
Decans: The Decans arc the thirty-six deities each of whom presides over ten degrees of the
zodiac. Sec in general, Gundcl, Dekane und Dekansternbilder; cf. also G. J. Turner, "Mathematics and Astronomy/' in J. R. Harris, ed., The Legacy ofEgypt (Oxford: Oxford University
Press, 2 1971) 46-53; 0. Neugebauer and R. A. Parker, Egyptian.Astronomical Texts, I (Providence and London: Brown University Press, 1960) 95-121. [R.K.R.]
Demokritos: Strangely, the philosopher of Abdera (fifth century B.C.) was thought in antiquity to have been involved in magic. See E. Wellmann, "Dcmokritos (6)," PRE 5 (1903):
135-40; I. Hammer-Jensen, PRE.S 4 (1924) :219-23; H. Steckle, PRE.S 12 (1970):
191-223, esp. 193-94, 199-200. See also Ostanes.
EI LANCHYCH formula: Forrhis magical formula, see PGMIII. 13lff.; IV. 1625, 1630 (with
corrupt or variant spellings). EI is perhaps Coptic for "house." [R.K.R.]
Eloaios: Eloaios occurs in PGM in various forms (Eloe, Elouein, Elouai) as a name for the
Jewish god (see PGMI. 311; IV. 1577; VIL 564; XXXVI. 42). In Gnosticism he is one ofrhe
light-aeons and is described as having a donkey's face. See J. Michl, RAC 5 (1965) 212, no.
73: Eloaios.
ERBETH formula: The formula "16 ERBETH, 16 PAKERBh'TH, 16 BOICJiosETH, 16 APOMPS"

book_title: The Greek Magical Papyri in Translation Including the Demotic Spells
text:
occurs quite often in magical texts, especially in malicious invocations. See Hopfncr, OZ II,
secs. 142-43.
Erebos: An old Greek expression for the dark underworld, the place of the dead. Sometimes
in literature it describes a place for the impious only, other times for the good bcl0re they are
admitted to rhe Elysian fields. See 0. Waser, "Erebos," PRE 6 (1907) :403-4.
Ereschigal: This name of the Babylonian underworld goddess is regularly associated with
the Greek Hekate. The deity. already occurs in the lead curse tablets of the fourth century B.C.
Erotylos: A writer ofOrphica (see PGM XIII. 945) by this name is not otherwise known
but may be the person mentioned by Zosimus in Bertholet and Ruelle, Collection des anciens
aJchimistesgrecques II (1888) 144, 7. See Kem, Orph. Fr. p. 71, no. 235; idem, "Erotylos,"
PRE.S 4 (1924): 386. For rhe possible Greek meaning of rhc word, consult LSJ s.v.; cf. also
PCM VIL 478; CXXIIla. 24 and comments by F. Maltomini, Studi classici e orientaJi 29
(1979): 76-77.
Esies: Esics (Egyptian l;sy, "praised") is an epithet of the sacred dead often applied to Osiris
who was drowned and restored to life. See S. Eitrem, "Tcrtullian de Bapt. 5. Sanctified by
Drowning," CIR 38 (1924): 69; A. Hermann, "Ertrinkcn/Errrankcn," RAC 6 (1966):
370-409; C. Strauss, LdA 2 (1977): 17-19.
Eulamo: For literature and a possible interpretation of this magical name, see H. C. Youtic
and C. Bonner, "Two Curse Tablets from Beisan," TAPA 68 (1937) :62; cf. PGMIII. 57;
VII. 401; IX. 8; XVI. 18.
Faience: Falence is a blue-green earthenware material popularly used in ancient Egypt for
jL-welry and other objects.
Good Daimon. See Agathos Daimon.
Hapi and Mnevis: The A pis (Hapi) and Mnevis bulls were incarnations of Ptah, Osiris, and
Ra, respectively. See Bonnet, BARG 46-51, s.v. "Apis"; 468-470, s.v. "Mncvis."
Harpocrates: Harpokrates ("Horus the child") typically is portrayed with a finger of his
right hand to his mouth, and he also may hold a crook and flail in his left hand. Harpo~tes
is the son of Isis and Osiris and is identified with the rising sun. Sec Bonnet, RARG
273-75, s.v. "Harpokrates"; D. Meek, "Harpokrates," LdA 2 (1977): 1003-11.
Harpon-Knouphi formula: This is Horus Knephis. On "Knephis" (Km-3tf) as the

Agathos Daimon, see LdA I, 94; II. 1011-12. For this as Horus Khnum (and on the fixmula in general), see P. Pcdrizet, "BRINTATEN◊PHRJS: I' un des noms magiqucs du <lieu
Chnoum,'' Melanges Maspero, II: Orientgrec, romain et byzantin 13 7 -44; G. M. El-Khachab,
"Some Gem Amulets Depicting Harpocratcs," ]EA 57 (1971): 132-33; D. Meeks, "Harponknuphi," LdA. 2 (1977) : 1011-12. [ R.K.R.]
Harsamosi: According to W.W. Schmidt, GGA 193 (1931): 452, the name is Egyptian /:{rsmsw, "Horus the Firstborn." See also PGM IL 155; XL 91-92; Xlll. 626; cf I. 240-41.
See D. Jankuhn, "Horsemsu," Ldli 3 (1980): 13.
Hathor: The Egyptian goddess of love; sec Blecker, Hathor and Thoth 22-105; F. Daumas
"Hathor," Ldli 2 (1977): 1024-33.
'
Headless One (GreekAkephalos): The Headless God is one of the most peculiar deities of
the PGM. His origin seems to be in the older Egyptian religion, but he became very popular
in Hellenistic Egypt, where he could be identified with Osiris (as in PGM IL 98-117) and
Besas (as in PGM VIL 222-49; VIII. 64-110). Headless deities are also known outside
Egypt. Plutarch tells about the headless Molos in Crete (Def orac. 417E), Pausanias of the
headless Triton in the temple of Dionysos at Tanagra (9. 20. 5); see A. Delatte, "Erudes sur
la magic grecquc V," BCH 38 (1914): 189-249; K. Preiscndanz, "Akephalos," RAC I
(1950) :211-16; K. Abel, "Akephalos," PRE.S 12 (1970): 9-14, with bibliography. For depictions of the god, sec Preisendanz, PGM vol. I, plate I, 2; Bonner, SMA 58, 110, 164-66,
178, 243; Delatte and Derchain, Les intailles 42-54.
Helios: The Greek word for the sun (Helios) can stand for the celestial body or for the deity
representative of that body. In the PGM, Helios is usually transcribed from Greek instead of
translated as "sun," unless that term seems completely devoid of the sense of a deity.
Helios-Osiris: Although this link is possible through the fusion with Sarapis, for the older
link of Osiris and Re, see A. Piankoff, TheLitanyofRe (New York: Bollingcn, 1964) 19-21.
Hephaistos: The important connection ofHephaistos, the Greek god of the hearth and of
fire, with magic is reflected a few times in PGM (sec VIL 379; XlL 177,417,439). Since
Herodotus, Hephaistos was the Greek interpretation of Ptah. See M. Delcourt, Hephaistos ou
la lcgende du magicien (Paris: Les belles lenres, 1957).
Hermop<>lis: Hcrmopolis is "the city of Hermes," the cult center of Thoth in upper
Egypt, the modern Ashmunein; cf. PGM III. 664; 670. See Bonnet, RARG 293-95, s.v.
"Hermopolis."
Hesies: See Esies.
Horus: The great Egyptian god, son of Osiris and Isis. Sec Bonnet, RARG 307 -15, s.v.
"Horus"; W. Schenkel, "Horus," Ldii 3 (1980): 14-25.
Iabas (Iabo, lab.µ, Iapos): This is apparently the Samaritan enunciation of the tetragrammaton YHWH (Yahweh), elsewhere rendered IaJ;e or Iabai; cf. PGMV. 102; Xie. I; Xll. 4
and S. Lowy, The Principles of Samaritan Bible Exegesis (Leiden: Brill, 1977) 273-74 and
passim. See also IAO.
IAEOBAPHRENEMOUN formula: This magical formula (often abbreviated) is intended to
read as the long palindrome IAE◊BAPHRENEMOUNOTHILARlKRIPHIAEYEAIPIRKIRALI­
THONUOMENERPHAB◊EAI; see PGMI. 140,195; III. 60-61 (var.), 77,268, etc.
IAO: Ia6, originally derived from the name of the Hebrew god YHWH, became an imp0rtant deity in magical literature. Sec J. Michl, RAC 5 (1965) :215, no. 102; R. Ganschinietz,
"IAQ," PRE 9 (1914) :698-721. In addition to being arrested in the Nag Harnmadi Library (sec Robinson, The Nag Hammadi Library in English, index), Ia6 is also found at
Qumran, 4Q Levb LXX; cf H. Stegemann, "Religionsgeschichtliche Erwagungcn zu den
Gottcsbczeichnungcn in den Qumrantcxtcn," in M. Delcor, ed., QumrtinJ sa piite, sa thioUJgie
et son milieu (Gembloux: Duculot, 1978) 195-217.
IARBATHA formula: A common magical name, which, when spelled out fully and with allowance for variant spellings, reads IARBATHACHRM:INEPHIBA6CHNf:ME6 (see PGMI. 142,
195; III. 472, 535; XII. 94-95). PHIBA◊CHNEME◊ may be equivalent to the Egyptian P3
bib c3 Ifnm c3, "the great lamb, Khnum the great." [R,K.R.]
Ieu (Jeu): The scribe )cu is mentioned only in PGM V. 97 (cf also I. 141) in PGM, but the

a god or magical name. See C. Schmidt, ed., and V. MacDermot, trans., The Books of]eu and
the Untitled Text in the Bruce Codex, NHSt 9 (Leiden: Brill, 1978).
Isis band: Cloth or material taken from the dresses of statues of the gods, especially of Isis,
was considered magically potent. Isis is a widow of Osiris and thus identified with the color
black. Sec PGM I. 59; VII. 227,231; VIII. 67; see Griffiths, Plutarch's De Iside et Osiride 90,
451; Hopfner, OZ!, sec. 678. [R.K.R.]
Jacob: The patriarch Jacob named at PGM XXIb. I, together with Abraham and Isaac in
XIII. 817, XXV. 14, occurs frequently in the context of magic. See Ginzberg, The Legends of
the Jews I, 349-58; M. Rist, "The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: A Liturgical and Magical Formula," JBL 57 (1938): 289-303.
Khnum (Chnurn): The Egyptian ram god; see PGMI. 27-28; IV. 327. Sec Bonnet, RARG
135-40, s.v. "Chnum"; E. Otto, "Chnum," Ldii. l (1975) :950-54.
Kmeph: The Egyptian serpent god Kmcph or K,neph occurs in PGM IV. 1705; III. 142; IV.
2094; VII col. 17 with picture. See Bonner, RARG 378-79, s.v. "Kneph."
Korn.mes: The name Kommcs is still unexplained (see also IL 122; cf. "Kommi" in XVI. 63;
Korn-Re in DMP xii, xv). See Gundcl, Dekane undDekansternbilder 233-34.
Lamella) pl. lamellae: From the Latin for a thin, metal plate. The word is used to translate a
number of Greek terms for tablets of thin gold, silver, iron, or lead. The lamcllac are usually
engraved and worn as amulets or talismans (phylacteries). If lead is described, the tablets
usually intend malicious or harmful magic.
Lamps, not painted red: In the PGM we find freguent references to the use of lamps with
no red coloring (sec I. 277,293; II. 57; IV. 2372, 3191; VII. 542,594; VIII. 87; XII. 27,
131; LXII. 1). Dipping the clay into red ocher (miltos) or painting it on before the firing, as
customarily done, would give the lamp a reddish color. In lamp divination, however, the red
color had to be avoided because of its association with Seth-Typhon. See W. Kroll, "Minium," PRE 15 (1932): 1848-54; R. Ganszyniec, "Lychnomanteia," PRE 13 (1927): 211519. Cf also DMP col. V, 4, pp. 44-45 (with note), where the lamp is said to be white,
without the appJication of red lead (pf"f). On the significance of red, cf G. Poscner, "Les
signes noirs dans !es rubriques,"JEA 35 (1949): 77-81. [R.K.R.J
MASKELLI-MASKELLO formula: This well-known formula, written fully as MASKELL! MASKELL◊ PHNOUK.ENTABA◊ OREOBAZAGRA RHEXICHTH()N HIPPOCHTH◊N PYRIPEGANYX, occurs often in magical literature (note PCM VII. 302; IX. 10; XXXVI. 342-46; DMP xv. 2;
Pistis Sophia IV, chap. 140 [McDcrmot 365]). On the meaning see Hopfner, OZ I, sec. 747;
Preisendanz, "Maskelli Maskcll6," PRE 14 ( 1930) : 2120. Within this formula, among other
things, occur four words which may be old Greek epithets: Oreobazagra, perhaps an epithet
of Hekatc or of the moon goddess (thus LS], but of uncertain meaning); Rhezichth0n, a
word which may be translated '"bursting forth from the earth" (thus LS]; see Cook, Zeus, 111
4-5 for parallels and discussion. Sec also Bonner, S.MA 170; Orph. H. 52. 9); Hippochth0n
(meaning unexplained, thus LS]: Audollent, Tab. Def 38129; cf Hermann, "Erdbcbcn,"
RAC 5 [1965]: 1082ff.); Pyripeganyx, perhaps "lord of the fount of fire" (LSJ s.v.; Audollent, Defixionum Tabellae 38. 29).
Material, magical: "Material" (ousia; sec PCM I. 99, IV. 2336, etc.) is the magical substance
such as hair, thread from clothing, etc., which is often necessary to make sympathetic magic
effective, Sec K. Prcisendanz, "Miszcllen zu den Zaubcrpapyri, I," WSt 40 (1918): 1-8;
Hopfner, OZ I, sccs. 667-77.
Meliouchos: The meaning of this epithet is still unexplained. In the magical texts it can be
attributed to various deities. Sec PCM III. 45-46, 99; V. 4; VI. 33; Audollcnt, Defixi,onum
Tabe/lae 22. 32; 38. 12; sec P. E. Gobel, "Meliuchos," PRE 15 (1931): 554-55.
Mene: This is an epithet of the moon goddess, Selene; sec Hymn. Hom. 32. l; Hymn. Orph.
9. 3, 4; PGM IV. 2264, 2546, 2815; VII. 758.
Mithras: The Persian god is mentioned only a few times in PCM (note III. JOO, 462; IV.
482) and each time as being identical with Helios or with Zeus~Hclios-Sarapis (sec PGM V.
4). Sec Nilsson, GGR II,668-72; Dieterich, .11ithrasliturgie67ff;M. J. Vcnnascrcn, "Mithras

text:
Moses: In Greco-Roman antiquity, Moses was widely recognized as a great magician. Sec
Gager, Moses in Greco-Roman Paganism 134-61.
Myrrh( ed.) ink: This ingredient used for ·writing on papyrus occurs throughout the PCM.
Cf. the note on the Demotic equivalent r' w !JI in DMP v. 5.
Nature (Greek Physis): Physis appears from early rimes as a deified conception of nature's
powers of creation and creativity. As such, Physis has an important role in most philosophical schools, especially where the concept of kata physin ("'in accordance with nature") seems
at times to rise almost to the level of a religious credo (so in Seneca, De Prov. IV. 15 and
often). Physis appears often elsewhere as a goddess: cf., for example, Hymn. Orph. 10 which
is addressed to Physis. Much of its language closely resembles that in the PCM hymns to the
moon (to whom Hymn. Orph. 9 is addressed). In PCM Physis the goddess appears elsewhere at IV. 2883, 2917; sec also IV 939 and n. The surprising thing is that she does
not appear more often in PCM. See K. Kerenyi, "Die G6ttin Natur," Eranos-]ahrbuch 14
(1947): 39-86.
NEBourosouALETH: The name occurs frequently in magical literature and is often connected with Aftiophis and Ereschigal. In PGM the triad is often attributed to deities of the
underworld, especially Hekate. The name Nebutosoualeth may be derived from the Babylonian god Nebo, but the origin is not clear. See K. Preisendanz, "Ncburosualeth," PRE 16
(1935) :2158-60; Bonner, SMA 30, 197-98.
Nephotes: The name appears to be a hellenized form of the Egyptian Nefer-hotep (Nfr/Jtp), but it is uncertain to whom it refers. Originally, it was the name of an Egyptian deity.
See A. Rusch, "Nephotes" PRE 16 (1935) :2493-94; cf Bonnet, RAR.G 518-19, s.v.
"Nephotcs." [R.K.R.]
(On)nophris: An epithet of Osiris, "The Beautiful Being." For the common proper name
Onnophris, see Preisigke, Namenbuch 242. Cf PGM IV. 1078; IV. 128. [R.K.R.]
Oserapis: The occurrence of the old name Oserapis (cf. PCM XL. l) for Serapis on the
fourth century B.C. curse found in the Serapeum of Memphis is important for the origins of
this cult. See on this issue Nil,;son, GGR II, 156. Cf. also the note on PGM XIXa. 6.
Osoronnophris: This is equivalent to the Egyptian Wsir Wn-nfr, "Osiris the Beautiful
Being"; cf. PGMV. 101 and IV. 1078. [R.K.R.l
Ostanes (Osthanes): The historical Ostanes was a theologian at the court of Xerxes, with
whom he went to Grec~e. He is said to have taught Dcmokritos the philosopher (who is also
mentioned in PGMN. 2006; VII. 167, 795; XII. 122,351) and to have introduced magic to
Greece (Pliny NH 30. 8). Later, many different writings were transmitted under the name of
Ostanes. See J. Bidez and F. Cumont, Les mages hellinisis. Zoroastre, Ostanis, et Hystaspe
d'apres la traditwngrecque (Paris: "Les belles lettres," 1938), vol. II, 267-356; K. Preisendanz, "Ostanes," PRE 18 (1942): 1610-42.
Ouroboros: The serpent who swallows its own tail is a widely used figure in magic. Sec
W. Deonna, "Ouroboros," Artibus Asiae 15 (1952): 163-70; K. Preisendanz, "Aus der
Gcschichte des Uroboros," in Brauch und Sinnbild. Eugen Fehrle zum 60. Geburstag gedwidmet von seinen Schiilern und Freunden (Karlsruhe: Kommissionsverlag Siidwestdeutschc
Druck- und Verlagsgesellschaft, 1940) 194-209. For examples of the figure on Egyptian
monuments, sec A. Piankoff, The Shrines ofTut-Ankh-Anwn (Princeton: Pantheon Books,
1955) pl. 48; idem, Mythological Papyri (Princeton: Pantheon Books, 1957) 22, fig. 3; 174,
fig. 74; papyri 20, 27. [R.K.R.] Sec PGM I. 145-46; XII. 203-4, 274-75; VII. 58-59;
XXXVI. 184.
Ouserrannouphthi: This is Egyptian Wsir-rn-nfr, "Osiris of the good name." [R.K.R.]
Palindrome: Palindrome (lit. "running back again") refers to magical words, usually of no
recognizable sense, which can be read and pronounced the same forward as backwards.
Persian: The epithet "Persia," used of Artemis-Hekare (cf PGM IV. 2271, 2715, 2781)
shows evidence of the identification of the goddess with the Persian goddess Anahita. Sec
Diod. V. 77 and Nilsson, GGR II, 672ff

Pitys: W. Bousset, Hauptprobleme der Gnosis (fG6ttingen: Vandcnhocck and Ruprecht,
1907] 192, n. I; cf. Religionsgeschichtliche Studien 59, 105,157,210) has suggested that the
Thcssalian Pitys named in PGM IV 1928, 2006, 2140 is in fact identical with the Egyptian
priest and prophet Bitys (Iamblichus, De myst. 8. 5; 10. 7), the Biros named in Zclsimos) On
the Letter Omega, and Bithus of D~rn-had1ium mentioned in Pliny, NH 28. 82. Sec FestugiCre, La RePilation I, 268; Nilsson, GGR II, 610; K. Prcisendanz, "Pitys (3)," PRE 20
(1950): 1882-83.
Phre: See Ra.
Phtha: Sec Ptah.
Phylactery: A phylactery (Greek phylakterion) in the PGM refers to any stone, material, papyrus amulet, or Iamdla, engraved ,virh a spell or othcnvise, ·which is ,vom about the person
for protection. The term should not be confused with the Jewish technical term referring to
the tefillin cases with Scripture verses.
Pnouthis: Pnouthis, or Pnythios, is an Egyptian name and means "He of God." See K. Preiscndanz, "Pnuthis," PRE 41 (1951): 1104.
Priestly papyrus: Or "hieratic papyrus" refers to the best quality of paper for the writing of
magical spells (c£ for example, PGM I. 233; IV 2363, 2512-13; VII. 412). For rhis technical distinction on the quality of papyrus, sec Lewis, Papyms in Classical Antiquity 43-45.
[R.K.R.]
Processional way (Greek komasterion): Ordinarily refers to the meeting place of the revelers of Dionysos, but in PGA,J it is used several rimes as a metaphor describing heaven as a
place of procession of the stars (see also l'GM N. 1608-9; XII. 184, 252; XIII. 774; XX.I.
IO; LX1.'VII. 13).
Psammetichos: The name is the hellenized form of the Egyptian name Psmtk. A legendary
figure, Psammetichos I (663-609 R.C.) was the first king of the twenty-sixth Dynasty, but
other figures also bore this name. See W. Heick, "Psammetichos," PRE 23 (1959): 1305-8.
Psyche: See Soul.
Punishments, the (Greek bai TimiJriai): These are the Greek deities responsible for retributive punishment and hence appropriately cited in spells dealing with malicious magic.
See PGM VII. 303; XIII. 149, 291, 457; and K. Ziegler, "Timoros," PRE 2nd scr. 6
(1937): 1308-9.
Ptah: This is the Egyptian creator god, for which see Bonnet, R.ARG 614-19, s.v. "Ptah."
Pythagoras: Because of his interest in the mysticism of numbers, this philosopher's name
became attached to late texts associated with mantic and magic. Sec W. Burkert, Lore and
Science in Ancient Pythagoreanism (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1972)
109ff.; idem, Griechiscbe Religion 445-47.
Ra (Re, Phre): The Egyptian god of the sun (P)re, wlthout the definite artjclc. Re means
simply "sun," while Pre, the form of the god)s name from the New Kingdom onward, means
"the Sun.·'-' See Bonnet, RARc 626-30, s.v. "Re."
Sarapis (Serapis): The god Sarapis, closely associated with Osiris in PGM IV. 226, appears
mostly in the PGA,f as identical with Zeus and Helios (see, e.g., IV 1715; V. 4-5; LXXIV.
4-5, 14, and Nilsson, GGR II, 513), but not with Dionvsos, with whom the Greeks identi~
ficd Osiris (Herod. 2. 42; Plut. Is. et Os. 356C). See G. Roeder, "Sarapis," PRE, 2nd scr. 2
(1920) 2394-2496; John E. Strambaugh, Sarapis under the Early Ptolemies, EPRO 25
(Leiden: Bril!, 1972); G. Mussies, "The lnterpretatio Judni.c.a of Sarapis," in M. J Ver~
mascren, ed., Studies in Hellenistic Religions, EPRO 78 (Leiden: Brill, 1979) 188-214;
L. Vielman, "Isis und Sarapis," in Die rtricntalischen Religionen im Riimcrreich 121-56. Sec
PGM XIXa. 6 and n.
Sachmou: This is the Egyptian goddess of war and plague (PCM VIL 300), Sakhmct; sec
Bonnet, RARG 643-46, s.v. "Sachmet." [R.K.R.]
Scarab: The bcctk (Ateucltus saccr) regarded as holy by the Egyptians and associated with
various deities. Sec Bonnet, RAR.G 720-22, s.v. "Skarabaus"; J. Assrnann, "Chcpre," LdA I
(1975) :934-40; J. Bergman, "Ancient Egyptian Theogony in a Greek Magical Papyms
(PGM VII, 11. 516-521)," in Studies in Eg_vptian Religion Dedicated to Professor Jan Zandee
(Leiden: Brill, !982) 28-37.

Selene: The Greek word for the moon (sclene) can stand for the celestial body or for the
deity representative of that body. In the PGM, Selene is usually transcribed from Greek instead of translated as "moon" unless that term seems completely devoid of the sense of dl..'.it\'.
SESENGENBARPHARANGES: A magical name very common in the PCM. It is often fi.)m{d
together with ABLANATHANALBA. for possible derivations of the name and further rdCrences, sec W. fauth, "SS.M PDRSSA," Zcitschnft dcr Deutschcn M01;genliindischcn Ccscllschaft
120 (1970) :229-56, esp. 254-55.
Seth: See Typhon/ Seth.
Soul: The word psyche occurs frequently in PCM where it usually means "soul," "mind," etc,
and "spiriLs of the dead." But in several passages (VI. 277, 2488; VII. 414,472; XV!la. 18)
psyche means female pudendum, i.e., a synon}m of physis, another regular term for the pudendum both in PC.M and elsewhere. In addition, there arc other places (i.e., IV. 1040
1526, 1752, etc.) ·where psyche is translated "soul;' but the erotic context also suggests th;
added meaning of pudendum. Indeed, it is entirely possible that such a double emendre was
the origin of the c,~ended meaning (see esp. IV. 1752, 2924; XXXII. 9, 15; XXXI!a. 15).
This meaning of psyche occurs also outside of PGM. See, e.g., Juvenal, Sat. 6. 193-99, esp.
195; Martial, Epitfr. 68. 5-12, esp. 5-7; and also Sophocles, El. 775. [E.N.O.]
Systasis: "Divine encounter," velsim. is a technical term for a rite (PCM IV. 778-79; VII.
505ff) or prayer (PGMIII. 197-98, 494ff; IV. 260ff.) to establish an association between a
god and a person. Sometimes the association is really only a meeting between the god and
the human in order for the human to receive a revelation (PCM III. 197:ff.; see 11. 192-96;
cf. also II. 43, 73; III. 698-99) or a blessing (see JI. 576ff in PGM III. 494ff, and in IV.
260ff., 11. 272 and 284-85). At other rimes, the association is to be more long-lasting, and
the god is to ally himself with the human (PGM I. 57, 79-80, 177-81) even to the point of
somcreaJ sort ofunion (PGMIV. 209, 219-21; cf. JI. 215-17; XIII. 927-31). There is no
single English word to encompass this variety of meanings, and therefore systasis and cognate
words are translated in a variety of ways throughout this volume. For a different interpretation of systasis, sec K. PrcisCndanz, "Miszellcn zu den Zauberpapyri," WSt 40 (1913): 2-5.
TIIERNOPSI formula: This formula in PGM III. 186, IV. 828-29, VIL 316 (with corruptions or variant readings) refers to the magical incantation "PSINOTHER NOPSTTHER THERNC>Psl." for possible Egyptian meaning, sec Hopfuer, OZ I, sec. 750. Note, however, that
the three words form rearranged groupings of the syllables PSI, NO, and THEIL [R.D.K.]
Thoth (Thouth, Thoouth, Theouth, Thooth): The Egyptian god of wisdom and magic,
whom the Greeks identified with Hermes. See Bonnet, RA.Re 805-12, s.v. "Thor"; P. Boylan, Thoth, the Hermes ofEgypt (Chicago: Ares, 2 1979), esp. 124ff.; G. Mussics, "The Interpretatio Judaica ofThot-Hcrmcs," in Studies in Egyptian RcligUJn, Dedicated to Professor Jan
Zandee (Leiden: Brill, 1982) 89-120.
Typhon/Seth: The identification of the Egyptian god Seth with the Greek Typhoios or Typhos was already made by the Greeks of the Classical period (Hesiod, Thcog. 820ff.) and was
common in the Greco-Roman Period (sec Plut. De ls. et Os. 2, 35lf and often), a fact reflected also in the PGAf (see, e.g., VIL 964; XII. 138; XIV. 20). For references, see Colpc,
RAC 9 (1974): 556-57, 620-21. Because the figure of Seth was believed to be donkeyheadcd, Typhon in PGM IV. 3260 and elsewhere (cf. Xla. 1-2; IV. 2220) probably means
"ass." See H. re Veldc, Seth, God ofConfusion (Leiden: Brill, 1967).
YESSIMMIGADON/AKROUROBORE formula: For this fonnula (with varianrs) sec PCM II.
32; IV. 277lff (cf. IV. 337); V. 424ff; VII. 680ff; 895ff; XIII. 923ff.; XIXa. 12; DMP vii.
25-26. In this formula, AKROUROBORE is believed to mean in Greek "carer of the tip of
your tail~ (thus LS]), a reference to the ouroboros (sec Glossary, s.v.). On the formula, sec
Drexler in Roschcr, I, 2. 2771; J.M. R. Omnack, "A TabellaDefixionis in the Museum of the
University of Reading, England," HTR 44 (1951) :25-34, esp. 31-32.
